claim: The evolutionarily conserved TRanscript-EXport (TREX) complex plays central roles during mRNP (messenger ribonucleoprotein) maturation and export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
source: The evolutionarily conserved TRanscript-EXport (TREX) complex plays central roles during mRNP (messenger ribonucleoprotein) maturation and export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: In yeast, TREX is composed of the THO sub-complex (Tho2, Hpr1, Tex1, Mft1, and Thp2), the DEAD box ATPase Sub2, and Yra1.
source: In yeast, TREX is composed of the THO sub-complex (Tho2, Hpr1, Tex1, Mft1, and Thp2), the DEAD box ATPase Sub2, and Yra1.
evidence: This claim describes the composition of the yeast TREX complex and is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: A 3.7 Å cryo-EM structure of the yeast THO•Sub2 complex was determined.
source: Here we present a 3.7 Å cryo-EM structure of the yeast THO•Sub2 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM data collection and processing described in the manuscript.

claim: The structure reveals the intimate assembly of THO revolving around its largest subunit Tho2.
source: The structure reveals the intimate assembly of THO revolving around its largest subunit Tho2.
evidence: This claim is based on the structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: THO stabilizes a semi-open conformation of the Sub2 ATPase via interactions with Tho2.
source: THO stabilizes a semi-open conformation of the Sub2 ATPase via interactions with Tho2.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the THO•Sub2 complex.

claim: THO interacts with the serine–arginine (SR)-like protein Gbp2 through both the RS domain and RRM domains of Gbp2.
source: We show that THO interacts with the serine–arginine (SR)-like protein Gbp2 through both the RS domain and RRM domains of Gbp2.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro binding studies and cross-linking mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Cross-linking mass spectrometry analysis supports the extensive interactions between THO and Gbp2.
source: Cross-linking mass spectrometry analysis supports the extensive interactions between THO and Gbp2, further revealing that RRM domains of Gbp2 are in close proximity to the C-terminal domain of Tho2.
evidence: This claim is supported by XL-MS experimental data.

claim: RRM domains of Gbp2 are in close proximity to the C-terminal domain of Tho2.
source: Cross-linking mass spectrometry analysis supports the extensive interactions between THO and Gbp2, further revealing that RRM domains of Gbp2 are in close proximity to the C-terminal domain of Tho2.
evidence: This claim is supported by XL-MS data showing cross-links between Gbp2 RRM domains and Tho2 C-terminal domain.

claim: THO serves as a landing pad to configure Gbp2 to facilitate its loading onto mRNP.
source: We propose that THO serves as a landing pad to configure Gbp2 to facilitate its loading onto mRNP.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TREX is recruited to actively transcribed genes.
source: TREX is recruited to actively transcribed genes (Cheng et al., 2006; Masuda et al., 2005; Strässer et al., 2002) and impacts transcription especially during elongation (Domínguez-Sánchez et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TREX impacts transcription especially during elongation.
source: TREX is recruited to actively transcribed genes (Cheng et al., 2006; Masuda et al., 2005; Strässer et al., 2002) and impacts transcription especially during elongation (Domínguez-Sánchez et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The C-terminal domain of the largest subunit of RNA Pol II is highly phosphorylated on the heptapeptide repeats (YSPTSPS) at the Serine 2 position during the elongation phase of the transcription cycle.
source: The C-terminal domain of the largest subunit of RNA Pol II is highly phosphorylated on the heptapeptide repeats (YSPTSPS) at the Serine 2 position during the elongation phase of the transcription cycle (Hsin and Manley, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Serine 2 phosphorylation coordinates loading of co-transcriptional 3'-end processing factors to the transcription machinery.
source: Serine 2 phosphorylation coordinates loading of co-transcriptional 3'-end processing factors to the transcription machinery (Ahn et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In yeast, the primary RNA Pol II CTD Ser2 kinase is the CTDK-1 complex.
source: In yeast, the primary RNA Pol II CTD Ser2 kinase is the CTDK-1 complex (Cho et al., 2001; Sterner et al., 1995; Wood and Shilatifard, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The yeast TREX component Mft1 interacts genetically with CTDK-1.
source: The yeast TREX component Mft1 interacts genetically with CTDK-1 (Hurt et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: TREX and CTDK-1 both influence mRNA 3'-end processing and polyadenylation.
source: In addition to their roles during transcription elongation, TREX and CTDK-1 both influence mRNA 3'-end processing and polyadenylation (Ahn et al., 2004; Rougemaille et al., 2008; Saguez et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In humans, at least CDK9, CDK11, CDK12, and CDK13 are shown to phosphorylate Ser2 on Pol II CTD.
source: In humans, the transcriptional kinases are more divergent, at least CDK9, CDK11, CDK12, and CDK13 are shown to phosphorylate Ser2 on Pol II CTD, among which CDK12 and CDK13 are orthologs of yeast CTDK-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: CDK12 and CDK13 are orthologs of yeast CTDK-1.
source: In humans, the transcriptional kinases are more divergent, at least CDK9, CDK11, CDK12, and CDK13 are shown to phosphorylate Ser2 on Pol II CTD, among which CDK12 and CDK13 are orthologs of yeast CTDK-1.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Human CDKs are recognized as potential targets for cancer therapy.
source: These human CDKs are recognized as potential targets for cancer therapy (Cao et al., 2014; Parua and Fisher, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TREX and CDK11 have been shown to interact in human cells and play roles in regulating HIV mRNA 3'-end processing.
source: TREX and CDK11 have been shown to interact in human cells and play roles in regulating HIV mRNA 3'-end processing (Pak et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In yeast, there are three shuttling SR-like proteins, Gbp2, Hrb1, and Npl3, which play roles in mRNA export by interacting with the mRNA export receptor Mex67•Mtr2.
source: In yeast, there are three shuttling SR-like proteins, Gbp2, Hrb1, and Npl3, which play roles in mRNA export by interacting with the mRNA export receptor Mex67•Mtr2 (Hackmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In humans, three SR proteins, SRSF1, SRSF3, and SRSF7, shuttle between the nucleus and the cytoplasm to facilitate mRNA export by serving as adaptors for the human ortholog of Mex67•Mtr2, the NXF1•NXT1 complex.
source: In humans, three SR proteins, SRSF1, SRSF3, and SRSF7, also shuttle between the nucleus and the cytoplasm to facilitate mRNA export by serving as adaptors for the human ortholog of Mex67•Mtr2, the NXF1•NXT1 complex (Huang et al., 2003; Huang and Steitz, 2005; Müller-McNicoll et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TAP-tagged Gbp2 and Hrb1 were shown to associate with the CTDK-1 complex in yeast cells.
source: In yeast cells, TAP-tagged Gbp2 and Hrb1 were shown to associate with the CTDK-1 complex (Hurt et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Gbp2 RRM domains are sufficient to interact with CTDK-1, involving the N-terminal RS domain in its Ctk1 kinase subunit.
source: Consistent with this observation, using purified recombinant proteins, we recently showed that Gbp2 RRM domains are sufficient to interact with CTDK-1, involving the N-terminal RS domain in its Ctk1 kinase subunit (Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: There is a synthetic growth defect when both CTK1 and GBP2 are knocked out in yeast.
source: We also found that there is a synthetic growth defect when both CTK1 and GBP2 are knocked out in yeast.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: In humans, CDK11 interacts with SRSF7.
source: Interestingly, in humans, CDK11 interacts with SRSF7 (Hu et al., 2003), and together with TREX, all are implicated in HIV-1 mRNA 3'-end processing (Pak et al., 2015; Valente et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CDK11, SRSF7, and TREX are implicated in HIV-1 mRNA 3'-end processing.
source: Interestingly, in humans, CDK11 interacts with SRSF7 (Hu et al., 2003), and together with TREX, all are implicated in HIV-1 mRNA 3'-end processing (Pak et al., 2015; Valente et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Gbp2 and Hrb1, but not Npl3 have been shown to rely on the THO components Hpr1 and Mft1 to load onto mRNPs.
source: Among the three yeast shuttling SR-like proteins, Gbp2 and Hrb1, but not Npl3 have been shown to rely on the THO components Hpr1 and Mft1 to load onto mRNPs (Häcker and Krebber, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There is an interaction between THO and Gbp2 and Hrb1, but not Npl3.
source: The different requirements could stem from an interaction between THO and Gbp2 and Hrb1, but not Npl3 (Hurt et al., 2004; Martínez-Lumbreras et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: THO directly interacts with Gbp2 using purified recombinant proteins.
source: Using GST pull down assays, we show that Gbp2 directly interacts with THO–FL (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: THO* is capable of binding to Gbp2, but with reduced interaction compared to THO–FL.
source: We found that THO* is capable of binding to Gbp2, but with reduced interaction compared to THO–FL (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Multiple regions in THO are involved in Gbp2 recognition, including both the THO core and the potentially flexible regions that are truncated in THO*.
source: These results suggest that multiple regions in THO are involved in Gbp2 recognition, including both the THO core and the potentially flexible regions that are truncated in THO*.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding data comparing THO-FL and THO*.

claim: Gbp2 without RRM3 still binds to THO.
source: Interestingly, we found that Gbp2 without RRM3 still binds to THO (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Deletion of the N-terminal RS domain of Gbp2 substantially reduced THO interaction.
source: On the other hand, deletion of the N-terminal RS domain of Gbp2 substantially reduced THO interaction, suggesting that the Gbp2 RS domain is required for stable binding to THO.
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The Gbp2 RS domain is required for stable binding to THO.
source: On the other hand, deletion of the N-terminal RS domain of Gbp2 substantially reduced THO interaction, suggesting that the Gbp2 RS domain is required for stable binding to THO.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding data showing reduced interaction when the RS domain is deleted.

claim: THO–Gbp2 interaction involves multiple domains from both THO and Gbp2.
source: Together, our binding studies indicate that THO–Gbp2 interaction involves multiple domains from both THO and Gbp2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding studies presented.

claim: The THO complex is an integrated structural and functional unit that regulates the activity of Sub2.
source: The THO complex is an integrated structural and functional unit that regulates the activity of Sub2.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior work and the structural data presented.

claim: A THO•Sub2 crystal structure at 6.0 Å resolution was previously determined.
source: We previously determined a THO•Sub2 crystal structure at 6.0 Å resolution (Ren et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The THO*•Sub2 complex was subjected to cross-linking with glutaraldehyde to obtain a more homogeneous sample for cryo-EM sample preparation.
source: For cryo-EM sample preparation, the THO*•Sub2 complex was subjected to cross-linking with glutaraldehyde to obtain a more homogeneous sample.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological step in the cryo-EM sample preparation.

claim: Full length THO complex isolated from yeast cells was shown to form a dimeric assembly by negative stain EM.
source: Full length THO complex isolated from yeast cells was shown to form a dimeric assembly by negative stain EM (Peña et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A higher ordered assembly composed of four THO*•Sub2 protomers was observed.
source: We observed a higher ordered assembly composed of four THO*•Sub2 protomers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in the supplementary figures.

claim: The THO*•Sub2 tetramer can be dissected as two dimers related by twofold symmetry.
source: This THO*•Sub2 tetramer can be dissected as two dimers related by twofold symmetry, Dimer 1 (protomer 1A and 1B) and Dimer 2 (protomer 2A and 2B).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM data.

claim: Within each dimer, a coiled-coil region (corresponding to Mft1 and Thp2) from each protomer interact via a 'head on' mode.
source: Within each dimer, a coiled-coil region (corresponding to Mft1 and Thp2) from each protomer interact via a 'head on' mode.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The interaction between the two dimers is mediated by the same coiled-coil region via a 'side to side' mode involving protomer 1A and 2A.
source: The interaction between the two dimers is mediated by the same coiled-coil region via a 'side to side' mode involving protomer 1A and 2A.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The recent structure of human THO in association with UAP56 also exhibits a tetrameric assembly.
source: It is interesting to note that the recent structure of human THO in association with UAP56, the human ortholog of Sub2, also exhibits a tetrameric assembly (Pühringer et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The 'head on' mode interaction is conserved between yeast THO•Sub2 and human THO•UAP56.
source: The 'head on' mode interaction is conserved between yeast THO•Sub2 and human THO•UAP56 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the yeast and human structures.

claim: Tetramerization of human THO•UAP56 is mediated by the Thoc6 subunit and a Thoc5 domain that do not exist in yeast.
source: However, tetramerization of human THO•UAP56 is mediated by the Thoc6 subunit and a Thoc5 domain that do not exist in yeast.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the yeast and human structures.

claim: XL-MS analysis of the full length THO in association with Gbp2 identified multiple cross-links between a 'bulge' (Mft1 a.a. 142–196) and Tho2 C-terminal region.
source: Our XL-MS analysis of the full length THO in association with Gbp2 (details in later section) identified multiple cross-links between a 'bulge' (Mft1 a.a. 142–196) and Tho2 C-terminal region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Supplementary file 2) that can only be explained by the interface between two protomers within a dimer, whereas no cross-links support the 'side to side' interface of the tetramer.
evidence: This claim is supported by XL-MS data.

claim: No cross-links support the 'side to side' interface of the tetramer.
source: Our XL-MS analysis of the full length THO in association with Gbp2 (details in later section) identified multiple cross-links between a 'bulge' (Mft1 a.a. 142–196) and Tho2 C-terminal region (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and Supplementary file 2) that can only be explained by the interface between two protomers within a dimer, whereas no cross-links support the 'side to side' interface of the tetramer.
evidence: This claim is supported by XL-MS data.

claim: The THO* core contains ~600 residues less than the full length THO complex.
source: Of note, the THO* core contains ~600 residues less than the full length THO complex.
evidence: This claim is based on the design of the THO* construct.

claim: Both full length THO isolated from yeast cells and the full length THO in association with Sub2 purified from recombinant proteins exhibit a dimer.
source: Given that both full length THO isolated from yeast cells (Peña et al., 2012) and the full length THO in association with Sub2 purified from recombinant proteins (Schuller et al., 2020) exhibit a dimer, we speculate that the THO*•Sub2 tetramer was formed due to the truncations in THO*.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The THO*•Sub2 tetramer was formed due to the truncations in THO*.
source: Given that both full length THO isolated from yeast cells (Peña et al., 2012) and the full length THO in association with Sub2 purified from recombinant proteins (Schuller et al., 2020) exhibit a dimer, we speculate that the THO*•Sub2 tetramer was formed due to the truncations in THO*.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison with full-length THO structures.

claim: Each THO*•Sub2 dimer contains a rigid protomer (1A or 2A) and a mobile protomer (1B or 2B).
source: Each THO*•Sub2 dimer contains a rigid protomer (1A or 2A) and a mobile protomer (1B or 2B) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The dimer observed by cryo-EM is consistent with the previously determined crystal structure which contains one THO*•Sub2 and a second THO*•Sub2 that is only partially resolved.
source: This dimer observed by cryo-EM is consistent with our previously determined crystal structure which contains one THO*•Sub2 and a second THO*•Sub2 that is only partially resolved (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D; Ren et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with prior structural work.

claim: The relative orientation between the protomers is flexible.
source: Comparison of the THO*•Sub2 dimer in our work and the recently reported structures of yeast THO•Sub2 and human THO•UAP56 reveals that the relative orientation between the protomers is flexible (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; Pühringer et al., 2020; Schuller et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of multiple structures.

claim: The THO*•Sub2 protomer was refined to an overall resolution at 3.7 Å.
source: For obtaining the best quality map for model building, the THO*•Sub2 protomer was extracted from the two rigid copies (1A and 2A) within the tetramer and refined to an overall resolution at 3.7 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM data processing workflow.

claim: The electron density map allows building an atomic model of the THO complex de novo.
source: The electron density map allows us to build an atomic model of the THO complex de novo (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by the quality of the cryo-EM map.

claim: Sub2 was modeled using the previously determined crystal structure.
source: Sub2 was modeled using our previously determined crystal structure (Ren et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim describes the modeling approach for Sub2.

claim: The THO model contains 2000 residues with 90% assigned residue register.
source: The THO model contains 2000 residues with 90% assigned residue register.
evidence: This claim describes the completeness of the atomic model.

claim: Tho2, the largest subunit spanning the entire length of the elongated THO, plays a critical role in THO assembly.
source: Tho2, the largest subunit spanning the entire length of the elongated THO, plays a critical role in THO assembly.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO complex.

claim: Tho2 can be dissected as 'head', 'neck', and 'trunk' sections.
source: Tho2 can be dissected as 'head', 'neck', and 'trunk' sections.

source: The Tho2 'head' contains an N-terminal helical bundle that clusters with the N-termini of Hpr1, Mft1, and Thp2.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO complex.

claim: Tho2 'neck' is comprised of a helix followed by a loop.
source: Tho2 'neck' is comprised of a helix followed by a loop.

claim: The 'neck' is embraced by a bi-lobed Hpr1 (lobe A and lobe B).
source: The 'neck' is embraced by a bi-lobed Hpr1 (lobe A and lobe B).

source: Tho2 'trunk' folds into an alpha solenoid structure, which binds the Tex1 β-propeller at its center and stabilizes a semi-open Sub2 ATPase at its C-terminal end.

claim: Tho2 'trunk' binds the Tex1 β-propeller at its center.
source: Tho2 'trunk' folds into an alpha solenoid structure, which binds the Tex1 β-propeller at its center and stabilizes a semi-open Sub2 ATPase at its C-terminal end.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO complex.

claim: Tho2 'trunk' stabilizes a semi-open Sub2 ATPase at its C-terminal end.
source: Tho2 'trunk' folds into an alpha solenoid structure, which binds the Tex1 β-propeller at its center and stabilizes a semi-open Sub2 ATPase at its C-terminal end.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO•Sub2 complex.

claim: An extended region at Hpr1 C-terminal region forms a 'belt' lining the Tho2 'trunk'.
source: An extended region at Hpr1 C-terminal region forms a 'belt' lining the Tho2 'trunk'.

claim: Tho2 features a total contact area of ~9000 Å2 with the other four THO subunits.
source: Tho2 features a total contact area of ~9000 Å2 with the other four THO subunits.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO complex.

claim: Tho2 'head' domain binds to a four helix bundle, formed by two pairs of anti-parallel helices contributed by Mft1 and Thp2, respectively.
source: Tho2 'head' domain binds to a four helix bundle, formed by two pairs of anti-parallel helices contributed by Mft1 and Thp2, respectively (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO complex.

claim: Tho2 'head' and the helix in its 'neck' sandwich the very N-terminal helix of Mft1 (residues 6–17).
source: Tho2 'head' and the helix in its 'neck' sandwich the very N-terminal helix of Mft1 (residues 6–17).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO complex.

claim: The opposite side of the Mft1/Thp2 four helix bundle runs in parallel with Hpr1 lobe A (residues 1–230).
source: The opposite side of the Mft1/Thp2 four helix bundle runs in parallel with Hpr1 lobe A (residues 1–230).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO complex.

claim: The Tho2 'neck', particularly the loop (residues 167–179), is embraced by the Hpr1 lobe A and lobe B (residues 250–490).
source: The Tho2 'neck', particularly the loop (residues 167–179), is embraced by the Hpr1 lobe A and lobe B (residues 250–490) (Figure 3B).

claim: The 'neck' contains multiple hydrophilic residues including K171, N173, and E177.
source: Although the 'neck' is largely buried, it contains multiple hydrophilic residues including K171, N173, and E177.

claim: Tho2 and Hpr1 residues at the 'neck' interface are highly conserved from yeast to human.

source: The 'trunk' of Tho2 (residues 180–1200) forms an alpha-solenoid.

source: Sub2-C makes contacts with two pairs of Tho2 helices (residues 625–695).

evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO•Sub2 interface.

claim: The ATPase activity of Sub2 mutant E356A/K357A/R358A cannot be activated by THO.
source: The importance of this loop is evidenced by our previous mutagenesis studies that show the ATPase activity of Sub2 mutant E356A/K357A/R358A cannot be activated by THO (Ren et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Sub2 assumes a closed conformation in its enzymatic active state, in which Sub2-N and Sub2-C clamp onto its RNA substrate.
source: Sub2 assumes a closed conformation in its enzymatic active state, in which Sub2-N and Sub2-C clamp onto its RNA substrate.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of DEAD-box ATPase mechanisms.

claim: The semi-open Sub2 is more similar to its active state than free Sub2 in which Sub2-N and Sub2-C are likely separated.
source: As we previously illustrated (Ren et al., 2017), the semi-open Sub2 is more similar to its active state than free Sub2 in which Sub2-N and Sub2-C are likely separated.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison and prior work.

claim: In vitro, the observed stimulation of Sub2 activity may reflect change in dynamics of switching between different conformational states as a result of THO binding.
source: In vitro, the observed stimulation of Sub2 activity may reflect change in dynamics of switching between different conformational states as a result of THO binding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the in vitro data.

claim: In cells, Sub2 is recruited to the transcription machinery via THO.
source: In cells, Sub2 is recruited to the transcription machinery via THO and the semi-open Sub2 may represent a 'primed' state that enables efficient transition to the active state when a physiological RNA substrate is encountered.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of TREX function.

claim: The semi-open Sub2 may represent a 'primed' state that enables efficient transition to the active state when a physiological RNA substrate is encountered.
source: In cells, Sub2 is recruited to the transcription machinery via THO and the semi-open Sub2 may represent a 'primed' state that enables efficient transition to the active state when a physiological RNA substrate is encountered.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the structural data.

claim: This Sub2 activation mechanism is a conserved mechanism shared by several other DEAD-box proteins including Dbp5.
source: This Sub2 activation mechanism is a conserved mechanism shared by several other DEAD-box proteins including Dbp5 which functions at the terminal step of nuclear mRNA export at the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear pore complex (Folkmann et al., 2011; Mathys et al., 2014; Montpetit et al., 2011; Schütz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dbp5 functions at the terminal step of nuclear mRNA export at the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear pore complex.
source: This Sub2 activation mechanism is a conserved mechanism shared by several other DEAD-box proteins including Dbp5 which functions at the terminal step of nuclear mRNA export at the cytoplasmic side of the nuclear pore complex (Folkmann et al., 2011; Mathys et al., 2014; Montpetit et al., 2011; Schütz et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The THO complex contains a significant amount of potentially flexible regions including ~400 residues at the Tho2 C-terminal end and ~150 residues at the Hpr1 C-terminal end.
source: The THO complex contains a significant amount of potentially flexible regions including ~400 residues at the Tho2 C-terminal end and ~150 residues at the Hpr1 C-terminal end.
evidence: This claim is based on the structural analysis showing these regions are not resolved in the cryo-EM structure.

claim: These flexible regions are presumably not suitable for structural studies.
source: These flexible regions are presumably not suitable for structural studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fact that these regions are not resolved in the structure.

claim: The flexible regions are involved in Gbp2 recognition.
source: Our binding studies show that these flexible regions are involved in Gbp2 recognition (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the binding data comparing THO-FL and THO*.

claim: A total of 200 unique EDC cross-links were obtained, of which 69 were interprotein cross-links including nine cross-links between Tho2 and Gbp2.
source: We obtained a total of 200 unique EDC cross-links, of which 69 were interprotein cross-links including nine cross-links between Tho2 and Gbp2.
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: A total of 133 unique DSS cross-links were obtained, with 53 of these cross-links being interprotein cross-links.
source: We also obtained a total of 133 unique DSS cross-links to complement the EDC cross-link data, with 53 of these cross-links being interprotein cross-links (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: The cross-linking data is highly consistent with the THO structure.
source: The cross-linking data is highly consistent with the THO structure (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the cross-link distances mapped onto the structure.

claim: 91% of the EDC cross-links that can be mapped to the structure fall within the expected distance restraint.
source: 91% and 100% of the EDC and DSS cross-links that can be mapped to the structure fall within the expected distance restraint.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the cross-link distances.

claim: 100% of the DSS cross-links that can be mapped to the structure fall within the expected distance restraint.
source: 91% and 100% of the EDC and DSS cross-links that can be mapped to the structure fall within the expected distance restraint.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the cross-link distances.

claim: XL-MS data provide experimental evidence to support the 'head on' THO–THO dimer.
source: As previously mentioned, our XL-MS data provide experimental evidence to support the 'head on' THO–THO dimer (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data showing cross-links consistent with the dimer interface.

claim: Multiple cross-links involving the Mft1 'bulge' and the C-terminal region of Tho2 unambiguously point to the THO–THO interface within the 'head on' dimer.
source: In particular, we identified multiple cross-links involving the Mft1 'bulge' and the C-terminal region of Tho2 (Mft1-K182/Tho2-K1103, Mft1-K165/Tho2-K967, Mft1-K170/Tho2-K967, and Mft1-K174/Tho2-K967) (Supplementary file 2). These cross-links unambiguously point to the THO–THO interface within the 'head on' dimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: The Tho2–CTD contains a 'bridge' that connects THO to the neighboring THO molecule as indicated by the cryo-EM density map.
source: The Tho2–CTD contains a 'bridge' that connects THO to the neighboring THO molecule as indicated by our cryo-EM density map (Figure 4B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM density map.

claim: The bridge starts at Tho2 residue 1200.
source: Comparison with the recently published THO–Sub2 structure reveals that the bridge starts at Tho2 residue 1200 (Schuller et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with another structure.

claim: The 'bridge' is followed by a structured segment, as suggested by the clustered cross-linking between Tho2 (residues 1260–1369) and the Hpr1 lobe B (E297, D434, K462, and K467) as well as Mft1 D129.
source: The 'bridge' is followed by a structured segment, as suggested by the clustered cross-linking between Tho2 (residues 1260–1369) and the Hpr1 lobe B (E297, D434, K462, and K467) as well as Mft1 D129 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: Tho2 (residues 1279–1405) was shown to form a rigid core through proteolysis and it folds into a helical structure as indicated by CD spectra.
source: In line with our observation, Tho2 (residues 1279–1405) was shown to form a rigid core through proteolysis and it folds into a helical structure as indicated by CD spectra (Peña et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cross-linking involving the structured segment indicates that the Tho2–CTD crosses over to the neighboring THO near its Hpr1 lobe B.
source: Importantly, cross-linking involving the structured segment indicates that the Tho2–CTD crosses over to the neighboring THO near its Hpr1 lobe B.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the XL-MS data.

claim: The structured segment is followed by a highly flexible tail (residues ~1400–1597), as this region cross-links to spatially separated residues.
source: The structured segment is followed by a highly flexible tail (residues ~1400–1597), as this region cross-links to spatially separated residues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the XL-MS data showing cross-links to distant residues.

claim: Tho2 K1576 cross-links to both Hpr1 lobe B (E297 and D434) and Tex1 (D341).
source: For example, Tho2 K1576 cross-links to both Hpr1 lobe B (E297 and D434) and Tex1 (D341).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: Tho2 (1411–1530) was highly sensitive to trypsin digestion.
source: In support of the flexibility of the Tho2 tail, a previous study showed that Tho2 (1411–1530) was highly sensitive to trypsin digestion (Peña et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both the THO•Sub2 structure and that recently published by others capture an asymmetric dimer exhibiting significant flexibility in the relative orientation of two THO•Sub2 molecules.
source: Both our THO•Sub2 structure and that recently published by others (Schuller et al., 2020) capture an asymmetric dimer exhibiting significant flexibility in the relative orientation of two THO•Sub2 molecules (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of multiple structures.

claim: The 'bridge' is only observed at the proximal side of the THO dimer.
source: The 'bridge' is only observed at the proximal side of the THO dimer.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis of the THO dimer.

claim: The Tho2–CTD will exhibit more significant flexibility at the distal side of the THO dimer.
source: It is conceivable that the Tho2–CTD will exhibit more significant flexibility at the distal side of the THO dimer.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural observations.

claim: The extensive cross-links observed between Tho2–CTD and Hpr1–CTD suggests that they are spatially close to each other and are likely localized in between two THO molecules.
source: The extensive cross-links observed between Tho2–CTD and Hpr1–CTD suggests that they are spatially close to each other and are likely localized in between two THO molecules.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the XL-MS data.

claim: Cross-linking between Tho2 and Gbp2 indicates that Tho2–CTD is in close proximity to all three Gbp2 RRM domains.
source: Cross-linking between Tho2 and Gbp2 indicates that Tho2–CTD is in close proximity to all three Gbp2 RRM domains (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: Each of the three RRM domains cross-links to the structured segment in Tho2–CTD: RRM1-K190 to Tho2-K1349, RRM2-E241 to Tho2-K1250, and RRM3-D367 to Tho2-K1335.
source: Each of the three RRM domains cross-links to the structured segment in Tho2–CTD: RRM1-K190 to Tho2-K1349, RRM2-E241 to Tho2-K1250, and RRM3-D367 to Tho2-K1335.
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: Gbp2 is localized in between two THO molecules near Hpr1 lobe B.
source: These results suggest that Gbp2 is localized in between two THO molecules near Hpr1 lobe B, as these involved Tho2 residues (K1250 and K1335) are cross-linked to Hpr1 lobe B (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the XL-MS data.

claim: Each RRM domain cross-links to the highly flexible tail in Tho2–CTD.
source: Our data also show that each RRM domain cross-links to the highly flexible tail in Tho2–CTD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the XL-MS data.

claim: In the presence of Gbp2, the Tho2 tail may assume a more specific conformation.
source: It is possible that, in the presence of Gbp2, the Tho2 tail may assume a more specific conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the XL-MS data.

claim: Tho2–CTD contributes to Gbp2 interaction.
source: Our XL-MS results (Figure 4C), together with the in vitro binding studies (Figure 1B and C), demonstrate that Tho2–CTD contributes to Gbp2 interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by both XL-MS and binding data.

claim: The C-terminal domain of Tho2 also binds to RNA/DNA.
source: The C-terminal domain of Tho2 also binds to RNA/DNA (Peña et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The function of Tho2–CTD in vivo was supported by the growth defect of tho2-ΔCTD yeast strains.
source: The function of Tho2–CTD in vivo was supported by the growth defect of tho2-ΔCTD yeast strains (Peña et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The synthetic growth defect of tho2-ΔCTD and Δgbp2 strains highlights their functional links.
source: Importantly, the synthetic growth defect of tho2-ΔCTD and Δgbp2 strains highlights their functional links (Martínez-Lumbreras et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: GST–Gbp2 is able to pull down both THO and Sub2, and THO and Sub2 appear to be in a stoichiometric amount relative to each other.
source: We found that GST–Gbp2 is able to pull down both THO and Sub2, and THO and Sub2 appear to be in a stoichiometric amount relative to each other (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data.

claim: GST–Gbp2 alone does not make direct contact with Sub2.
source: In addition, GST–Gbp2 alone does not make direct contact with Sub2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data.

claim: THO, Sub2, and Gbp2 can form a THO•Sub2•Gbp2 complex.
source: Our results suggest that THO, Sub2, and Gbp2 can form a THO•Sub2•Gbp2 complex, and therefore Gbp2 could function together with the TREX complex during nuclear mRNP maturation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the binding data.

claim: Gbp2 could function together with the TREX complex during nuclear mRNP maturation.
source: Our results suggest that THO, Sub2, and Gbp2 can form a THO•Sub2•Gbp2 complex, and therefore Gbp2 could function together with the TREX complex during nuclear mRNP maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the binding data.

claim: Gbp2 interaction with CTDK-1 provides a means to associate with the transcription machinery.
source: Gbp2 interaction with CTDK-1 provides a means to associate with the transcription machinery (Hurt et al., 2004; Xie et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TREX and Gbp2 function coordinately during nuclear mRNP maturation and surveillance.
source: We envision that TREX and Gbp2 function coordinately during nuclear mRNP maturation and surveillance.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented.

claim: Gbp2 and Hrb1 were shown to play key roles in mRNP surveillance.
source: In yeast, Gbp2 and Hrb1 were shown to play key roles in mRNP surveillance (Hackmann et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Interactions between Gbp2 and Mex67 for export and between Gbp2 and Mtr4 for degradation through the RNA exosome complex are mutually exclusive.
source: Interactions between Gbp2 and Mex67 for export and between Gbp2 and Mtr4 for degradation through the RNA exosome complex are mutually exclusive.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: TREX travels with the transcription machinery.
source: TREX travels with the transcription machinery (Meinel et al., 2013) and its function in mRNP assembly is well documented.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In THO/Sub2 mutant yeast cells, mRNP assembly is defective and faulty mRNPs cannot be degraded efficiently, which leads to the formation of heavy chromatin.
source: In THO/Sub2 mutant yeast cells, mRNP assembly is defective and faulty mRNPs cannot be degraded efficiently, which leads to the formation of heavy chromatin (Rougemaille et al., 2008; Saguez et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In humans, depletion of TREX complex components leads to R-loop accumulation, transcriptional elongation defects, and trapped mRNP in nuclear speckles.
source: In humans, depletion of TREX complex components leads to R-loop accumulation, transcriptional elongation defects, and trapped mRNP in nuclear speckles (Dias et al., 2010; Domínguez-Sánchez et al., 2011; Pérez-Calero et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: THO could serve as a landing pad for Gbp2 loading onto mRNPs to function as a key surveillance factor during mRNP maturation.
source: The extensive interactions between THO and Gbp2 suggest that THO could serve as a landing pad for Gbp2 loading onto mRNPs to function as a key surveillance factor during mRNP maturation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented.

claim: Both Gbp2 and the TREX complex component Yra1 serve as adaptors for the export receptor Mex67•Mtr2 to facilitate its loading onto mRNPs.
source: Both Gbp2 and the TREX complex component Yra1 serve as adaptors for the export receptor Mex67•Mtr2 to facilitate its loading onto mRNPs (Hackmann et al., 2014; Stutz et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Evidence suggests that the human THO complex also makes direct contact with the export receptor.
source: In humans, evidence suggests that the human THO complex also makes direct contact with the export receptor (Viphakone et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Yra1 contains a second Sub2 binding site at its N-terminus.
source: Interestingly, Yra1 contains a second Sub2 binding site at its N-terminus (Strässer and Hurt, 2001; Zenklusen et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: One Yra1 can engage with two Sub2 ATPase molecules in the THO•Sub2 complex.
source: It is plausible to speculate that one Yra1 can engage with two Sub2 ATPase molecules in the THO•Sub2 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural data and prior knowledge.

claim: In humans, SR proteins and Alyref bind to overlapping sites on the export receptor.
source: In humans, SR proteins and Alyref, the ortholog of Yra1, bind to overlapping sites on the export receptor (Huang et al., 2003), suggesting that Gbp2 and Yra1 may not act together to load Mex67•Mtr2.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Gbp2 and Yra1 may not act together to load Mex67•Mtr2.
source: In humans, SR proteins and Alyref, the ortholog of Yra1, bind to overlapping sites on the export receptor (Huang et al., 2003), suggesting that Gbp2 and Yra1 may not act together to load Mex67•Mtr2.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the human data.

claim: The multimeric THO complex can provide a platform to engage with both Gbp2 and Yra1, with each of them recruiting one Mex67•Mtr2 molecule.
source: Intriguingly, the multimeric THO complex in principle can provide a platform to engage with both Gbp2 and Yra1, with each of them recruiting one Mex67•Mtr2 molecule.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural data.

claim: THO may engage with Gbp2 and Yra1 during different stages of mRNP maturation.
source: Alternatively, THO may engage with Gbp2 and Yra1 during different stages of mRNP maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim.

claim: THO functions as a general platform to recruit multiple export factors.
source: Overall, our work supports a view that THO functions as a general platform to recruit multiple export factors, but further investigations are needed to pinpoint how THO spatially and temporally coordinates the actions of different export factors to prepare mRNPs for export.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data presented.
